title: FTC Part 1: The Slope of the Area

steps.body:
Push the accumulation forward a hair. From x to x + h you gain a sliver of area — and that sliver is very nearly a rectangle of width h and height f(x).

So A(x + h) − A(x) ≈ f(x)·h. Divide by h and let h → 0:

**A′(x) = f(x).**

Differentiation and integration are inverse operations. That is the Fundamental Theorem, and it is why they are taught together.
Watch the slope of A equal the height of f.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x². Sweep out an area of exactly 9 — and keep one eye on the tangent to the accumulation curve.
widget.successFeedback: x = 3, area 9 (since A(x) = x³/3). And read the line under the graph: the slope of A at x = 3 is 9 — while the HEIGHT of f at x = 3 is also 9. Not close. Equal. A′ = f, everywhere, always. The area function's derivative is the function you started with, and that is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
widget.lowFeedback: Not enough area yet. Keep dragging — and watch the accumulation curve steepen as f gets taller.
widget.highFeedback: Past 9. Come back — and notice how much faster A climbs out here, because f is so much taller.

predict.prompt: You'll sweep out area under f(x) = x² from the left. As x moves right, the accumulated area grows…
predict.reveal: Area pours in at exactly the current height of f(x) = x² — and that height keeps rising, so the accumulation curve bends upward. The rate the area grows IS the function's height.

cml.actionGoal: Move an upper bound and coordinate accumulated area with the integrand's current value.

explanationVariants: FTC Part 1 says d/dx[∫ₐˣ f(t) dt] = f(x). The integral sign and the derivative sign annihilate each other, leaving f with x substituted in.
You do not have to compute the integral at all. That is the entire point of the theorem.

options.label: x³
options.feedback: Right — the derivative undoes the accumulation, leaving the integrand with x written in. You never had to work out the integral.

options.label: x⁴/4
options.feedback: That is the accumulation itself (up to a constant). Differentiating it takes you back to x³.

options.label: 3x²
options.feedback: That is the derivative of the INTEGRAND. The theorem says the derivative of the INTEGRAL is the integrand itself, undifferentiated.
The lower limit being 1 shifts A by a constant, and constants have zero derivative — so it changes nothing at all. The answer is x³.

steps.body: The lower limit does not matter.
explanationVariants: Changing the lower limit from 1 to 5 shifts A by a constant (the area between 1 and 5), and a constant has zero derivative. So A′ is still f.
Different lower limits give different accumulation functions — but all of them have the SAME derivative.

widget.prompt: How does d/dx[∫₅ˣ t³ dt] compare with d/dx[∫₁ˣ t³ dt]?

options.label: They are identical — both are x³. The lower limit only shifts A by a constant.
options.feedback: Right, and that is the seed of the +C you are about to meet: the accumulation is pinned down only up to a constant.

options.label: They differ by 4.
options.feedback: The FUNCTIONS differ by a constant (the area from 1 to 5), but their DERIVATIVES do not differ at all — a constant differentiates to zero.

options.label: The second is larger.
options.feedback: Their values differ; their slopes are the same. Only the slopes are being asked about here.

options.label: You cannot compare them.
options.feedback: You can, and the answer is pleasing: both derivatives are x³.

steps.body:
With the chain rule, the upper limit can be anything:

**d/dx[∫ₐ^(g(x)) f(t) dt] = f(g(x))·g′(x)**

The accumulation is being swept at a rate g′(x), so the area piles up that much faster. It is the gears again.

explanationVariants: Here g(x) = x², so the answer is f(x²)·2x = (x²)³·2x = 2x⁷.
Substitute the upper limit into the integrand, then multiply by the derivative of the upper limit. That second factor is the chain rule, doing its usual job.

options.label: 2x⁷
options.feedback: Right: f(x²) = (x²)³ = x⁶, times the inner derivative 2x, gives 2x⁷. The chain rule charges for the moving endpoint.

options.label: x⁶
options.feedback: That is f(g(x)) with no inner derivative. The upper limit is racing along at rate 2x, so the area accumulates 2x times faster.

options.label: 6x²
options.feedback: That differentiates the integrand, which the theorem never asks you to do. Substitute the limit into f, then multiply by g′.

options.label: x⁸/4
options.feedback: That is the accumulation itself. The question asks for its DERIVATIVE, which is 2x⁷.

steps.body: Find the minimum of an accumulation.
hints: A′(x) = f(x) by the theorem — so to find where A turns, set f to zero.
f(x) = x² − 9 is zero at x = ±3. Only x = 3 is in [0, 5].
Check it is a minimum: f is negative before 3 and positive after, so A falls then rises.
explanationVariants: A′(x) = x² − 9 = 0 at x = 3 (within [0, 5]), and f changes from negative to positive there — so A has a minimum at x = 3.
You never computed A. The theorem let you find the turning point of an accumulation by looking only at the thing being accumulated.

widget.prompt: A(x) = ∫₀ˣ (t² − 9) dt on [0, 5]. At what x is A smallest?

commonErrors.feedback: A(0) = 0, but A then goes NEGATIVE, because t² − 9 is negative for t < 3. The minimum comes later.
By x = 5 the positive area has been piling on. A′(5) = 25 − 9 = 16 > 0, so A is climbing there, not bottoming out.
That is where the integrand is zero as a number, not where x makes it zero. Solve t² − 9 = 0: t = 3.

widget.fallbackFeedback: A′ = x² − 9 = 0 → x = 3, and f flips from negative to positive there: a minimum.

takeaways: A′(x) = f(x): the slope of the accumulation IS the height of the function.
So d/dx[∫ₐˣ f(t) dt] = f(x) — the two operations annihilate, and you never compute the integral.
The lower limit only shifts A by a constant, and constants have no slope.
steps.teaser: Next: run the theorem the other way, and it becomes a machine for computing areas.

concept.body: Push the endpoint forward by h and you gain a thin sliver of area — nearly a rectangle, width h and height f(x). So the area grows at the RATE f(x). That is all the theorem says: **A′ = f**.

explanationVariants: d/dx[∫₀ˣ t² dt] = x². The derivative undoes the integral.
The integrand comes back untouched, with x substituted for t.

options.label: x²
options.feedback: Right — the two operations cancel and hand back the integrand.

options.label: 2x
options.feedback: That differentiates the integrand. The theorem says do NOT differentiate it: the derivative of the integral IS the integrand.
